I've found that one of the best ways to learn a language is through immersion. I'm sure many of you folks know this already, but I'd like to share some of my tips regarding this.

If you use social media often, see if the website has a fully complete translation for the language you're trying to learn. I will often switch back and forth between English and Deutsch on my various accounts, and, believe it or not, I learn a great deal of Vokabular und Grammatik from this!

In addition, if any of you play video games, you'll find it not only interesting but fun to translate your game to German. By the time you do this, you will have most likely memorized certain names, actions, and buttons in the game, yet at first you will have to go to them via knowledge of their location. Afterwards, you will then translate and start to remember the German version of the tongue.

Furthermore, reading both prose text and news websites in German helps as well!

The next time you're on a site or playing a game you're quite familiar with, consider becoming acquainted in German!

Eeeep!! No!

The number of people in a poll has much less relevance than you'd think. Let's say you have a box of a billion red and blue marbles and want to know the percent breakdown of each color. The amount of marbles that you draw is actually not anywhere near as relevant as making sure you're drawing the marbles randomly. If we just have a bag full of them assorted in a truly random fashion and we pick out a 1000 or whatever then we're going to be able to draw some very accurate conclusions. However, in reality people and demographics end up clumping. So if you just draw from one section of the bag you might, for instance, end up getting far more red marbles than you would with better sampling. Draw a 1000 truly random marbles from that bag is going to be far more indicative than drawing a million marbles without ensuring they're actually representative, and it's incredibly tough to make sure that they're truly representative.

So for instance presidential elections are one of the hardest to poll for because politically demographics seriously clump, so getting a truly random and representative sample is tough. But the actual numbers we end up using are actually quite small. For instance here is a list of Gallup's polling performances which links to many of their reports where you can see the sample sizes used. You can see their numbers generally tend to be incredibly close to the actual results. Yet go click on a specific race result and you can see that their sample sizes tend to be around 3,000. And that's for something that's incredibly tough to get representative samples on, thus you end up needing a far larger sample size that would be necessary for more straight forward and well distributed polling topics.

That's the reason polling is so incredibly challenging. You can't just ask 'enough' people and then suddenly have a meaningful result. In fact, somewhat paradoxically, even polling every single person in a population on a question might end up not telling you the 'right' answer since there could be a bias in the people that choose to participate. It's a tough and incredibly poorly understood science.
